top.line: Build code review on fractal grammar, company-owned layers
top.para: Seven reader questions, answered by a voice memo of 5 October 2026, become a plan for a company built on code review. The fractal part is the grammar; each company decides its own layers. One technology can now read every layer, moving review from opinion and power to facts, if models build the graphs and then leave the line.

s0.line: Models build the graphs; deterministic checks then review changes
s0.para: The opening summary condenses the whole argument into one place. It runs through one reader for every layer, review as science, a fractal grammar with company-owned layers, projected and derived graphs joined by review, refactors relative to a held layer, the deploy as a layer, Wardley stages, sorting by reach, budgets, the five whys, and open source.

s1.line: One reader can now cover strategy down to bytecode
s1.para: Good reviewers always moved between altitudes by instinct, but no tool could read every layer, so earlier attempts to link requirements to code needed different tools and teams, and their hand-kept joins died. A language model reads a board objective, a story, a class and a syntax tree alike, making a graph at every layer buildable.

s2.line: Graphs and the map turn review into facts
s2.para: Code review has been an art shaped by taste and power because there was no fact base; the Wardley map and the graph supply one, saying where the code is and what a change reaches. Models should build the graphs, then leave the line. Budgets per altitude give an objective good enough, and production confirming the review is the test.

s3.line: The grammar is fractal; each company owns its layers
s3.para: Quoting the July 2026 architecture brief, fractal means self-similarity, scale invariance, composition and recursion: nodes, typed edges with inverses, ontology, taxonomy and zoom. Which layers exist, and their names, belong to the company's culture, languages and stack. A product that standardises layers loses what it reviews; the generic part is the grammar, tools and a few workflows.

s4.line: Review joins a projected graph with a derived one
s4.para: Stories and architecture project a graph downward before code exists; code derives one upward from the syntax tree. The join has three outcomes: a match, a node derived but not projected (a bug or unwritten story), and one projected but not derived (the plan or something forgotten). Progress is the count of projected nodes with a derived match.

s5.line: The example had the middle layers; prose skipped them
s5.para: The commit changed seven methods in two classes, two modules and two packages, reaching nine of seventy-two commands and six of eleven stories. The figure showed every layer, but the text jumped from methods to stories, a writing fault. Middle layers matter because each has a different reader, and modules and packages have fewest, which is why architecture drifts.

s6.line: Stories should be rules and examples, not prose
s6.para: The reader was right that prose stories were weak, and pointed to Example Mapping, described by Matt Wynne in December 2015: story, rules, examples and questions. In the graph a story roots rules whose leaves are examples linked to tests or runs, and question cards become pre-code findings. Matching tests by execution, not guesswork, moves up the vault's list.

s7.line: A refactor holds one chosen layer while others move
s7.para: The first article wrongly said a refactor leaves class shapes untouched; the general rule is that some layers move and one, the layer with the tests or contract, holds. Tidying a method holds the class shape, while an architecture migration holds the client interface, proved by contract tests. Review checks whether the claimed held layer actually held.

s8.line: Deploys and infrastructure are layers with their own vocabulary
s8.para: Pipelines, environments, services, configuration and secrets form a graph with verbs like deploys-to and assumes, and a blast radius continues through it, so a config change can reach further than any method. Non-functional requirements live at this altitude, held on nfrs.sgit.ai as measured claims. The deploy edge from explorer to villager environments is itself a review.

s9.line: Who reads the code depends on its Wardley stage
s9.para: Following Wardley's explorers, villagers and town planners and the March 2026 article Who should be reading the code: agents read explorer code, people read fully mapped villager code, and deterministic checks guard town planner code at the boundary. The company sits in the two moves between stages, avoiding both blind trust in models and reviewing everything by hand.

s10.line: Review sorts changes by reach rather than saying no
s10.para: The review tool should reshape a change before anyone reads it. Parts reaching no behaviour, like generated docs, merge on a deterministic check; parts on tested paths get checks and a one-line summary; mission-critical parts go to the right people. A hallucinated API bug in the Villager phase was caught only by a person reading the code.

s11.line: Replicate reality first, then argue about the facts
s11.para: Derive deterministically what a parser can, let a model propose the rest marked as proposed, then correct the graph with users, experts and tests. Synthetic users should run against the projected graph before code; the September site run recorded forty-three steps, fifteen unanswered questions and ten confusions. Every version is kept, so reviews can be replayed against past graphs.

s12.line: Budgets cap cost; the five whys make review cheaper
s12.para: Each altitude and change gets a budget declared in advance, and agents run under behaviour policies limiting what they read, write and spend. Onboarding starts at one point and grows along walked paths. Every finding asks why at the layer below, and the fix becomes a graph query rule, so checks grow until commodity review is almost entirely deterministic.

s13.line: Compare blast radius to intent, one line per layer
s13.para: The baseline is the intent, not the old code: the projected graph, commit message, pull request description, story and existing documentation. The report gives one line per layer that moved, saying whether it matches intent, and flags unmentioned layers. Progress on a big feature is the count of projected nodes with a derived match, visible weeks before customers see anything.

s14.line: Open source is the only business model that fits
s14.para: The layers belong to the customer and the loop must run where the code is, so locking customers into vendor layers would fight them. Following the Send strategy briefs, everything is open; the business sells the customised deployment, the running loop, the accumulated rules and the record. The parser, the model and the grammar are not for sale.

s15.line: Three corrections to the first article, and open questions
s15.para: The refactor rule is the held layer; the seven altitudes were one repository's layers; the example skipped commands and modules. Still open: no projected graph built from a brief, rules matched to tests by execution, no derived deploy layer, and no review tool yet. The next day a build brief, Code review graphs in the repository, set out the requirement.

s16.line: ChatGPT's infographic of the article checks out as faithful
s16.para: Dinis fed the article to ChatGPT for an infographic, checked against the text. Every element appears as the article has it and nothing was invented. Two quoted lines, "same reader, every altitude" and "standardise the grammar, not the customer's worldview", are the other model's fair condensations rather than sentences from the article.

s18.line: Sources: the studies, briefs and pages cited
s18.para: The main sources are Dinis Cruz's articles from 2025 and 2026, including Who should be reading the code, and Simon Wardley's posts on pioneers and explorers. Also cited: Matt Wynne's Introducing Example Mapping, Taiichi Ohno's Toyota Production System, the SecDevOps Risk Workflow book, open-source.sgit.ai, and many SG/Send briefs in the public team record.
